client: I've been really struggling to get anything done since my grandma passed away last month. I sit down to work on assignments but just end up staring at my notes while my mind drifts to memories of her. The sadness hits me out of nowhere sometimes, and I'm starting to worry I'll never get back to normal.
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling both deeply sad and a bit overwhelmed by these waves of grief—your voice sounds rushed and higher than usual, like the emotions are really pressing in on you right now. Let’s explore what "getting back to normal" means to you—could it be that expecting yourself to function as before might be adding pressure during an already tender time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I guess I hadn't thought about it that way. "Normal" to me means being able to focus at work without crying at my desk, but you're right - maybe that's not fair to expect right now. It's just hard because I feel like I'm failing at everything - grieving and working at the same time.
therapist: I hear how torn you feel between honoring your grief and meeting work expectations—your voice sounds tense but also more settled as you start to reconsider these standards you've set for yourself. What would it look like to gently acknowledge that you're actually holding two important things right now, rather than failing at either?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually makes me feel a little less guilty when you put it that way. But I still worry about practical stuff - my boss keeps asking why my productivity is down, and I don't feel comfortable telling him the real reason. It's like I'm stuck between being honest and keeping my job.
therapist: I notice your voice gets quieter and higher when you talk about work—it sounds like this situation is making you feel vulnerable and torn. Have you considered that there might be a middle ground between full disclosure and complete silence that could honor both your grief and professional needs?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could say I'm dealing with personal stuff, but I'm scared he'll think I'm making excuses. Part of me wants to just push through and pretend everything's fine, but that's exhausting too. I don't know how to find that balance between being professional and being human.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hesitant and urgent—like this dilemma is really weighing on you. It’s understandable to feel torn between protecting your job and honoring your grief, but pushing through completely might leave you even more drained. What would it feel like to acknowledge that being professional *can* include being human, especially during such a difficult time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That idea makes me nervous because my workplace has always felt so... corporate, you know? Like emotions don't belong there. But maybe I'm projecting - I don't actually know how my boss would react. It's just terrifying to imagine being vulnerable at work.
therapist: I hear that nervousness in your voice—it gets higher and pulls back when you talk about workplace vulnerability, like you're bracing for rejection. That fear makes complete sense given what you've described about your workplace culture, but notice how your voice also softens when you acknowledge you might be projecting—that openness might be a good starting point.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: You're right that I might be making assumptions, but I don't even know how to start testing that theory. The thought of saying anything at all makes my stomach clench - what if it backfires? Maybe I should just wait it out until I feel stronger.
therapist: Your voice sounds both anxious and determined—higher and stronger than before—as you weigh these risks, which tells me how much courage it would take to try this. While waiting until you feel stronger is one option, let's also acknowledge that strength often comes through small steps—what would be the gentlest way you could test these waters?

client: Maybe I could start by just saying I'm going through a tough time personally, without details? But even that makes me feel exposed. I'm worried if I open that door even a little, I might blurt out everything and look unprofessional.
therapist: I can hear the tension in your voice—it sounds both rushed and a bit higher-pitched as you wrestle with this idea, like just considering it makes you feel exposed. client: There's one woman in accounting who's always been kind - she brought me tea when she noticed I was upset that one time. But I'm scared if I open up to her, I'll start depending on her too much. What if she pulls back because she doesn't want to be my therapist at work?
therapist: Your voice sounds both hopeful and apprehensive—it rises noticeably when you recall her kindness, but tightens with worry about being a burden. What if sharing with her could simply be about human connection rather than dependency—might there be a middle ground that honors both your needs and hers?

client: That actually helps reframe it for me - I don't have to make it this big emotional unloading. Maybe just saying "I'm going through a loss" would be enough. But I still worry she'll pity me or treat me differently. I hate feeling like the sad person in the office.
therapist: I hear how conflicted you feel—your voice sounds both quick and a bit higher-pitched, like this worry about being seen as "the sad person" is really pressing on you.
